N-mixture family for repeated counts of unmarked individuals

Source: R/families.R
nmix.Rd

For counts made on repeated visits to sites whose abundance stays fixed across the visits, such as bird point counts within a season. The data hold one row per visit. The visits sharing a series and a time belong to one closure unit, whose latent abundance N is Poisson with mean mu. Each visit's count depends on N and the detection parameter p. The likelihood sums over N from the unit's largest count up to the cap K_max (Royle 2004).

Usage

nmix(
  type = c("poisson_binomial", "royle_nichols", "poisson_poisson"),
  multi_season = FALSE
)

Arguments

type

The variant, "poisson_binomial" by default. See Choosing a variant.

multi_season

Logical. TRUE keys a closure unit on (series, site, time), for several seasons of visits to each site. The data then need a site column, which pivot_detection_array() creates from a four-dimensional array with multi_season = "hierarchical". Each unit holds the visits of one site in one season.

Value

A family object to pass to mvgam() or jsdgam().

Details

bf(y ~ elev, p ~ tod) models abundance and detection, each with its own formula. mu takes the log link. predict() with type = "latent_state" gives the expected abundance of each unit given its counts. type = "detection" gives the detection probability of each visit.

Choosing a variant

All three variants take N ~ Poisson(mu) and differ in what a visit records.

"poisson_binomial" (Royle 2004)

Counts y ~ Binomial(N, p), which never exceed N. Point counts, removal passes and plot tallies fit this design. p is the detection probability of each individual, on the logit link.

"royle_nichols" (Royle and Nichols 2003)

Detections y ~ Bernoulli(1 - (1 - p)^N) in 0 / 1. Camera-trap or eDNA detections scored as present or absent fit this design. p is the detection probability of each individual, on the logit link. A visit's detection probability rises with N.

"poisson_poisson" (Neyman 1939)

Counts y ~ Poisson(N * p), which can exceed N. Camera-trap events and acoustic detections, where one individual is recorded several times, fit this design. p is the encounter rate of each individual per visit, on the log link.

Priors

A detection probability p on the logit link takes beta(1, 1) as a scalar. With a formula, its intercept takes normal(0, 1.5), which puts most of the probability between 0.05 and 0.95. The encounter rate of "poisson_poisson" takes lognormal(0, 1) as a scalar. With a formula, its intercept takes std_normal(). Either puts most of the rate between 0.14 and 7.4 encounters per visit. get_prior() lists these defaults. prior(..., dpar = "p") replaces one. A rare species might take prior(normal(-2, 0.5), class = Intercept, dpar = "p").

Identification

The counts identify abundance and detection apart through repeated visits and through covariates that act on one of them. With one visit per unit and no covariate, the data identify only the product mu * p. nmix() refuses that model. More than 30% of units visited once raises a warning. A "poisson_poisson" model with intercepts alone separates mu from p only through the extra variance of its counts. It warns. An informative prior on one intercept separates them.

Overdispersed abundance, such as negative binomial counts fitted by a Poisson N, biases abundance up and detection down, leaving their product close to the truth (Knape et al. 2018). pp_check() with type = "fit_stat" tests the per-unit totals for such misfit.

The cap on abundance

A cap column, constant within each unit and at least its largest count, sets the cap K_max. Without one, "poisson_binomial" and "poisson_poisson" take each unit's largest count plus 100, as unmarked::pcount() does. "royle_nichols" takes a fixed 25, as unmarked::occuRN() does. Its 0 / 1 detections carry no count to build a cap from. A lower cap shortens the sum and speeds sampling. A cap that binds biases abundance down. latent_N_saturation() reports, for each unit, the posterior probability that N equals its cap. A prediction frame may carry its own cap.

Joint species models

jsdgam() with nmix() or occ() fits several species at once. Latent factors shared by the species enter the state mu. p keeps its own formula. factor_formula = ~ s(env, by = lv_axis()) lets each factor follow an environmental gradient.

Importing array data

Detection histories from unmarked, spOccupancy or ubms come as a site-by-visit matrix, an array with species or seasons as further dimensions, or a list of matrices. pivot_detection_array() converts any of these to the long format, broadcasting site, season and visit covariates to their rows.

Threading

The density sums over units through Stan's reduce_sum(). Fitting with threads = 2 or more splits the units across threads.

References

Royle, J. A. (2004). N-mixture models for estimating population size from spatially replicated counts. Biometrics, 60, 108-115. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2004.00142.x

Royle, J. A. and Nichols, J. D. (2003). Estimating abundance from repeated presence-absence data or point counts. Ecology, 84, 777-790. doi:10.1890/0012-9658(2003)084[0777:EAFRPA]2.0.CO;2

Neyman, J. (1939). On a new class of "contagious" distributions, applicable in entomology and bacteriology. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 10, 35-57. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177732245

Knape, J., Arlt, D., Barraquand, F., Berg, A., Chevalier, M., Part, T., Ruete, A. and Zmihorski, M. (2018). Sensitivity of binomial N-mixture models to overdispersion. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 9, 2102-2114. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13062

See also

occ() for the related joint-occupancy family and pp_check.mvgam() for closure-unit goodness-of-fit checks. The N-mixture article fits N-mixture and occupancy models from data preparation to inference. The data article sets out the row layout that nmix() expects.

Other observation families: beta_nb(), categ(), com_binomial(), diri(), multi(), mvgam_families, mvn(), mvt(), occ(), tweedie()

Examples

# \dontrun{
# Counts at 50 sites, each visited four times. The state `mu` is
# the expected abundance and `p` the detection probability.
set.seed(5)
simdat <- sim_closure_unit_data(family = nmix(), n_species = 1L,
                                n_sites = 50L, n_visits = 4L,
                                type = 1L)
mod <- mvgam(
  bf(y ~ env, p ~ tod_c),
  data   = simdat$data_train,
  family = nmix(),
  chains = 2,
  silent = 2
)
summary(mod)
#>  Family: nmix 
#>   Links: mu = log; p = logit 
#> Formula: y ~ env 
#>          p ~ tod_c 
#>    Data: simdat$data_train (Number of observations: 200) 
#>   Draws: 2 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1; 
#>          total post-warmup draws = 2000
#> 
#> == Observation Model ==
#> Regression Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
#> Intercept       0.25      0.14    -0.02     0.52 1.00     1685     1600
#> p_Intercept     0.48      0.19     0.09     0.83 1.00     1443      918
#> env             0.09      0.12    -0.15     0.33 1.00     2110     1673
#> p_tod_c         0.06      0.04    -0.02     0.14 1.00     1808     1686
#> 
#> Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
#> and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
#> scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).
#> 
#> Next steps:
#>   - `pp_check(fit, type = "fit_stat")`: goodness of fit of unit totals
#>   - `plot(hindcast(fit, type = "latent_state"))`: posterior abundance of each unit
#>   - `forecast(fit, newdata = ...)`: out-of-sample forecasts
#>   - `loo(fit)` / `loo_compare(...)`: model fit + comparison
#>   - `conditional_effects(fit)`: covariate effects
#> Use `how_to_cite(fit)` for a methods paragraph and `methods_md(fit)` for its equations.

# Abundance and detection, separated by the model
head(predict(mod, type = "latent_state"))
#>      Estimate Est.Error Q2.5 Q97.5
#> [1,]   1.0560 0.2385214    1     2
#> [2,]   2.0805 0.2775937    2     3
#> [3,]   3.1135 0.3415788    3     4
#> [4,]   1.1105 0.3321821    1     2
#> [5,]   1.0500 0.2179995    1     2
#> [6,]   0.0330 0.1786812    0     1
head(predict(mod, type = "detection"))
#>       Estimate  Est.Error      Q2.5     Q97.5
#> [1,] 0.6815371 0.05912045 0.5660061 0.7897099
#> [2,] 0.6069331 0.04494594 0.5091557 0.6904690
#> [3,] 0.5373793 0.07305650 0.3918252 0.6766916
#> [4,] 0.6350496 0.04462901 0.5402543 0.7164926
#> [5,] 0.6514227 0.04807929 0.5541580 0.7396605
#> [6,] 0.6346711 0.04457818 0.5399661 0.7159861
plot(hindcast(mod, type = "latent_state"))


# A goodness-of-fit test on the per-site totals. A Bayesian p-value
# near 0 or 1 marks a misfit.
pp_check(mod, type = "fit_stat", stat = "freeman_tukey",
         ndraws = 200L)
#> Posterior predictive check (closure-unit discrepancy)
#>   Family:           nmix
#>   Statistic:        Freeman-Tukey
#>   Aggregation:      closure unit
#>   Posterior draws:  200
#>   Bayesian p-value: 0.235
# }
